baseline.title: The premise: the elections were already secure
baseline.sub: Every action on this page is justified as a response to fraud, above all voting by noncitizens. Before judging the response, measure the problem. Here is what the people who looked hardest found. Most of them are Republicans.

stats.label: Suspected noncitizen votes, 2016
stats.detail: The Brennan Center asked election officials in 42 jurisdictions across 12 states, covering 23.5 million votes and 8 of the 10 jurisdictions with the largest noncitizen populations. About 30 cases were referred for investigation. In 40 of the 42 jurisdictions, the number was zero.

stats.label: Credible impersonation cases in one billion ballots
stats.detail: Loyola law professor Justin Levitt tracked every credible allegation of in-person voter impersonation from 2000 to 2014. A separate News21 review of 2,068 alleged fraud cases since 2000 found 10 impersonation cases, about one for every 15 million voters.

stats.label: Noncitizens Georgia found on 8.2 million registrations
stats.detail: Republican Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger's October 2024 audit, which he called "the most comprehensive citizenship check ever conducted in Georgia." Nine of the 20 had ever voted. A September 2026 audit of 7.9 million registrations found the rolls more than 99.9 percent accurate.

stats.label: Trump's DOJ in court demanding state voter rolls
stats.detail: About thirty suits against 29 states and D.C., and twenty-one straight losses as of August 6, 2026. Twelve of the first twenty came from Republican-appointed judges, eight of them Trump appointees. A federal judge in Oregon wrote that the presumption of regularity the government normally enjoys "no longer holds."

rows.looked: What already stops a noncitizen from registering or voting
rows.found: A sworn citizenship attestation on every form, a federal database check, and up to a year in prison plus deportation.
rows.detail: The National Voter Registration Act requires every applicant to attest to citizenship under penalty of perjury (52 U.S.C. 20508). States check registrations against the Department of Homeland Security's SAVE database; that check is how Georgia caught every noncitizen who tried to register. Voting as a noncitizen is a federal crime under 18 U.S.C. 611 and makes the voter deportable without a conviction.

rows.who: CISA, Attorney General Barr, and about 60 courts
rows.found: "The most secure in American history." No fraud "on a scale that could have effected a different outcome." One minor court win in roughly 60 cases.
rows.detail: The joint statement of November 12, 2020 was signed by Trump's own cybersecurity agency and the bipartisan associations of state election officials: "There is no evidence that any voting system deleted or lost votes, changed votes, or was in any way compromised." Georgia counted its ballots three times, by hand and by machine. Michigan's Republican-led Senate Oversight Committee: "no evidence of widespread or systematic fraud."

rows.looked: About $1.5 million paid to two research firms to find fraud in five swing states
rows.found: "No reason to believe the final vote totals in five key states were fraudulent." The reports were never released.
rows.detail: Berkeley Research Group and Simpatico Software were hired by the campaign after the election. Ken Block of Simpatico: "Every fraud claim I was asked to investigate was false." The Associated Press separately reviewed the six battleground states and found fewer than 475 potential fraud cases against Biden's combined margin of 311,257 votes.

rows.who: Cyber Ninjas, hired by Arizona Senate Republicans
rows.looked: A hand count of 2.1 million Maricopa County ballots
rows.found: Biden gained 360 votes on the official count.
rows.detail: The review Trump's allies commissioned and promoted found Biden with 99 more votes and Trump with 261 fewer than the certified canvass.

rows.who: Georgia Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger (R)
rows.looked: Every registration since 1997, checked against the federal SAVE database
rows.found: 1,634 noncitizens tried to register in 25 years. None were added to the rolls. None voted.
rows.detail: From the secretary's own release: "All 2,258 individuals were placed in pending status and not added to the voter rolls. None of these individuals have cast ballots in Georgia elections." The existing checks caught every one.

rows.looked: More than 600 referrals from the secretary of state, out of 8 million registered voters
rows.found: Six indictments. "Not enough that it would have changed any of those elections."
rows.detail: Only 138 referrals alleged illegal voting; all six people indicted were lawful permanent residents, and one had died two years earlier. Yost: this "should enable everybody to take a deep breath and be more confident that our elections are, in fact, safe and secure." Ohio prosecutors said the referrals "often lack minimal evidence necessary to pursue charges."

rows.who: Iowa Secretary of State Paul Pate (R)
rows.looked: 2,176 voters challenged two weeks before Election Day; 1.6 million votes cast
rows.found: 277 confirmed noncitizens and 35 counted ballots. Nearly nine in ten of those challenged were citizens.
rows.detail: The federal SAVE check Pate later obtained confirmed 277 of the 2,176 as noncitizens, about 12 percent. Thirty-five noncitizen ballots were counted and five rejected, in an election of roughly 1.6 million votes.

rows.looked: Announced 6,500 noncitizens removed from the rolls, about 2,000 with a voting history
rows.found: 581 had been identified as noncitizens. The rest had not answered a letter. At least nine U.S. citizens were wrongly removed.
rows.detail: ProPublica, the Texas Tribune and Votebeat traced the numbers to the secretary of state's own report. The governor's press release was later edited to say "potential noncitizens."

rows.who: Alabama Secretary of State Wes Allen (R)
rows.found: A federal judge found an apparent error rate above 50 percent. At least 717 citizens were purged.
rows.detail: Judge Anna Manasco, a Trump appointee, wrote that Allen "later admitted that his purge list included thousands of United States citizens" and blocked the program for violating the National Voter Registration Act's 90-day quiet period.

rows.looked: A Motor Vehicle Commission software error, 2023 to 2024
rows.found: About 6,600 noncitizens registered by mistake and about 400 voted. The state found and reported it. Trump said the number was 35,152.
rows.detail: This is the largest confirmed case on record, and it belongs here. The registrants were Democrats, Republicans and mostly unaffiliated, and the governor said there was "no evidence at this time that any elections were swayed." FactCheck.org found the president's figure more than five times the state's.

rows.who: Trump's own Justice Department and DHS
rows.looked: A national hunt for noncitizen voters among 150 million 2024 ballots
rows.found: Fewer than 150 referrals, 41 charged, 14 convictions through May 2026. DHS claimed 16,000 noncitizens on Nevada's rolls and confirmed 185.
rows.detail: ProPublica's count from court records. The department's own maximal figure, given to the Daily Signal in September 2026, is 50 charged and 17 convicted since January 2025. Pennsylvania said DHS "did not have high confidence" in its list of 14,576 names; New Jersey and Pennsylvania asked for documentation DHS did not provide. A Minnesota federal prosecutor: "The entire process has been dysfunctional."

rows.looked: A raid on Fulton County's election office (600 boxes of 2020 ballots), a Maricopa subpoena, and home visits to Milwaukee officials
rows.found: "I promise you, it's coming soon." No arrests, no evidence released, and the acting attorney general will not promise "a definitive answer."
rows.detail: Patel told Fox News on April 19, 2026 that arrests over 2020 were imminent. As of June, the Atlanta Journal-Constitution reported the Fulton investigation had "failed to deliver so far." Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche: "I'm not going to promise that there's going to be a definitive answer."

baseline.take: The administration's case rests on a fraud that the people best placed to find it cannot find. Republican secretaries of state audited their own rolls and found cases in the dozens, in states with millions of voters. Trump's own campaign paid for a search and buried the answer. His own Justice Department has lost twenty-one straight suits for voter data, and his own prosecutors have produced fourteen convictions by ProPublica's count, seventeen by the department's own, out of a hundred and fifty million voters. Errors exist, and we list the biggest one above, because New Jersey found it and said so. What the record does not contain is the thing every card on this page is justified by. When the stated problem is this small and the response is this large, the response is the point.

saveact.title: The SAVE Act, in the data
saveact.sub: The president calls it a "National Emergency." He held a housing bill hostage for it and demanded the Senate kill the filibuster to pass it. Here is what the bill requires, who it would stop, and what happened the one time a state tried it.

stats.label: Citizens without ready access to proof of citizenship
stats.detail: 9.1 percent of voting-age citizens, in a 2023 survey by the Brennan Center and the University of Maryland. About 3.8 million have no such document at all. 11 percent of citizens of color lack ready access, against 8 percent of white citizens.

stats.label: Citizens without a valid passport
stats.detail: A passport is the simplest document the bill accepts. State Department data put valid passports at 0.48 per person. Fewer than a third of adults hold one in West Virginia, Mississippi, Alabama, Arkansas, Kentucky, Louisiana and Oklahoma; about one in five earning under $50,000 does.

stats.label: Kansans blocked from registering under the same rule
stats.detail: The only state to run a comparable law, 2013 to 2018. The blocked applicants were 12.4 percent of new registrations. Kansas could show 39 confirmed noncitizens registered over 14 years, 0.002 percent of voters. The Tenth Circuit struck the law down; the Supreme Court declined to hear the appeal.

stats.label: Registrations done in person today
stats.detail: About 80 million Americans register or update a registration each cycle; fewer than 6 percent do it at an election office. The bill requires anyone using the mail form to present papers in person, and makes every other method conditional on documents at the time of application.

rows.claim: "The SAVE America Act will ensure that our federal elections are decided by U.S. citizens, and U.S. citizens alone."
rows.who: Rep. Chip Roy and Sen. Mike Lee, sponsors, January 29, 2026
rows.found: Noncitizen registration is already a federal crime, and every state that has looked has found it in the dozens, not the thousands.
rows.detail: Kansas: 39 confirmed noncitizen registrations in 14 years, a share a federal appeals court called "statistically indistinguishable from zero." New Hampshire: 8 noncitizen cases in 8.3 million ballots cast from 1998 to 2024, per the judge who struck down its 2024 proof-of-citizenship law. Utah: one noncitizen among about 1.8 million active voters. Alaska: 70 possible cases since 2015.

rows.claim: "Anyone with a REAL ID can avoid them."
rows.who: National Review, on the bill's document hurdles
rows.found: A standard REAL ID does not show citizenship, so the roughly 140 million already issued would not qualify on their own.
rows.detail: The bill accepts a REAL ID only if it "indicates the applicant is a citizen of the United States." Most states' cards do not. Sen. Lisa Murkowski, who supports voter ID and opposes this bill: "Alaska's REAL IDs do not, so you would need to present a passport, certified birth certificate or another valid document." A military ID qualifies only with a service record showing a U.S. birthplace.

rows.claim: Married women who changed their name can use a birth certificate and an affidavit.
rows.who: The bill's defenders, and PolitiFact's March 2026 check
rows.found: True of the 2026 text, and worth saying plainly. It still puts a new step between roughly 69 million women and the registration form.
rows.detail: Pew found 79 percent of married women took their husband's surname. The Center for American Progress estimates about 69 million women hold a birth certificate that no longer matches their legal name. The 2026 bill lets a state accept "additional documentation" or a signed affidavit for a prior name, through a process each state must build under Election Assistance Commission guidance due 10 days after enactment. PolitiFact's verdict: the bill "doesn't eliminate voting rights but adds procedural hurdles."

rows.claim: "There are accommodations for those who don't have documentation."
rows.found: The accommodation is an in-person visit, and an election official who registers someone without papers commits a new federal crime.
rows.detail: Mail applicants "shall not be registered" unless they present documents "in person" at an election office. The bill adds "registering an applicant to vote ... who fails to present documentary proof of United States citizenship" to the list of federal election offenses and lets private parties sue the official. Republican county clerks in Idaho warned of a "mass exodus of poll workers." Alaska's Murkowski: registering "could mean purchasing plane tickets," with a two-month wait for certified documents. The rules take effect the day the bill is signed.

rows.claim: "The American people support it by an 80/20 margin."
rows.found: The Republicans who would have to run it, and the party's own editorial pages, do not.
rows.detail: Utah Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson (R): the bill "would be impossible to implement," and "I can count on zero fingers the number of times Sen. Lee has reached out to ask how his bill will affect our state." National Review: "it is prudent not to swat a fly with a sledgehammer... think dozens, not thousands." The Wall Street Journal editorial board called ending the filibuster for it "a terrible trade." Sen. Thom Tillis called it "theater." Five of six Idaho county clerks quoted by the Spokesman-Review, all Republicans, oppose it. The Senate has rejected it five times in 2026, twice at 48-50, with Collins, Murkowski, McConnell and Tillis joining every Democrat.

rows.claim: "The desperately needed SAVE AMERICA ACT, which I consider to be a National Emergency."
rows.who: Trump, canceling a housing-bill signing, June 24, 2026
rows.found: Two federal courts have ruled the president cannot impose the rule himself. What followed was leverage, not evidence.
rows.detail: His March 2025 executive order directing proof of citizenship on the federal form was permanently blocked in October 2025 ("the President lacks the authority to direct such changes") and again in June 2026 (the Constitution "does not grant the President any specific powers over elections"). He then refused to sign the ROAD to Housing Act, which passed 358-32 and 85-5, until the Senate passed the SAVE Act; it became law without his signature on July 11. On July 25 he posted: "Terminate the Filibuster... and PASS THE SAVE AMERICA ACT." In March he told Republican lawmakers that the mail-ballot ban he wants added to it is "the only way to guarantee the midterms."

saveact.take: Voter suppression is a strong phrase, so here is the standard we hold it to: a rule that stops far more eligible citizens than ineligible ones, adopted with that ratio in plain view. Kansas ran the experiment. It blocked 31,089 registrations to catch a few dozen noncitizens over two decades, and a federal appeals court called the noncitizen share statistically indistinguishable from zero. The SAVE Act is the Kansas rule for the whole country, effective the day it is signed, with a federal crime attached for the clerk who lets someone through. The people most likely to lack a passport or a matching birth certificate are the young, the poor, the rural, women who changed their name, and voters of color. The president has told Republican lawmakers what the package is for: to "guarantee the midterms." We take him at his word.

asked.title: Asked, and wouldn't rule it out
asked.sub: When officials have been asked directly whether armed agents, troops or emergency powers will be used around the midterms, these are the answers. Declining to rule something out is not a plan, so the last column records the denials and assurances the administration has given on the same question.

rows.asked: NBC's Tom Llamas asked whether he would trust the results of the midterms if Republicans lose control of Congress.
rows.answer: "I will if the elections are honest." Moments earlier, of the states that count votes: "If they can't do it honestly and it can't be done properly and timely, then something else has to happen."

asked.take: Several of these questions already have a one-line answer on paper, like General Caine's letter. The officials asked in person have mostly declined to repeat it. A threat does not need to be carried out to keep a voter home, which is why three lawsuits now argue that refusing to rule out armed agents at the polls is itself the harm.

heard.kicker: Predictions you may hear that we can't yet substantiate
heard.title: What you may have heard
heard.sub: Some fears about the midterms run ahead of the record. Each one is stated here the way people put it, then set against what is documented, what stands in the way, and what would have to happen for us to report it as fact. We hold these to the same standard as a claim of voter fraud.

items.claim: Trump will cancel or postpone the midterms.
items.record: The fear has a source. In January Trump told Reuters, "when you think of it, we shouldn't even have an election," and the White House said he was "simply joking." Asked in August and September about declaring an election emergency, he said "stranger things have happened" and "I don't rule anything out or in." The emergency proposals on the record would change the rules of the vote, such as voter ID and mail ballots, not its date, and we have found no reported order, draft or bill that would move it. One state did stop a federal election midway: Louisiana's governor suspended its U.S. House primaries in May to redraw the map, discarding ballots already cast. Those voters, he said, "will vote again in November."
items.stands: Federal law sets the date: "The Tuesday next after the 1st Monday in November, in every even numbered year" (2 U.S.C. 7). The Constitution gives the rules for congressional elections to state legislatures and to Congress (Art. I, Sec. 4), not to the president. The 20th Amendment ends House terms "at noon on the 3d day of January" whether or not anyone has been elected, so a delay would keep nobody in office. The Congressional Research Service: "there is no current constitutional authority residing in the President of the United States, nor the executive branch of government, to postpone, cancel, or reschedule elections for federal office in the various states."
items.would: A presidential order or proclamation that tries to change when or whether the election is held, or a bill in Congress to move it.

items.claim: He'll declare martial law, or use the Insurrection Act to stop the vote.
items.record: Asked by TIME on September 28 whether he would rule out a state of emergency before the midterms, Trump said, "I don't rule anything out or in," brought up the Insurrection Act himself, and said, "I've never used it. I could use it." National Guard troops are scheduled to stay on the streets of Washington, D.C., through Inauguration Day 2029. No invocation of the Insurrection Act and no order sending troops to polling places has been documented. Gen. Dan Caine, chairman of the Joint Chiefs, wrote to a senator in August that there are "no plans to send Federal military personnel or Federalized members of the National Guard to polling places during the 2026 elections."
items.stands: No law lets a president declare martial law. The Brennan Center: "There are no existing federal statutes that authorize the president to declare martial law," and "The Insurrection Act does not authorize martial law." That Act lets a president use troops "to enforce those laws or to suppress the rebellion" (10 U.S.C. 252), and first requires a proclamation ordering insurgents "to disperse and retire peaceably to their abodes within a limited time" (10 U.S.C. 254). It says nothing about elections. Separately, bringing "any troops or armed men" to a polling place is a federal crime "unless such force be necessary to repel armed enemies of the United States" (18 U.S.C. 592).
items.would: A proclamation under 10 U.S.C. 254, which must come before troops are used, or an order sending federal troops or federalized Guard into a state near Election Day.

items.claim: Hegseth is purging the generals to set up a military coup.
items.record: The purge is real. Hegseth has fired or blocked the promotions of "more than 80 generals and admirals," about 10 percent of the military's top officers, the New York Times reported. The reasons on the record point elsewhere: the Army secretary resigned after objecting to Hegseth "firing the generals who were responsible" for his modernization plans. And in August the leaders of three combatant commands and the Chief of Naval Operations formally objected, in writing, to orders extending the Iran war. We have found no reporting that ties the firings to the election.
items.stands: The officers themselves are bound by law. It is a federal crime for "an officer or member of the Armed Forces" to prevent "any qualified voter" from voting or to interfere with an election officer's duties (18 U.S.C. 593). The Posse Comitatus Act bars using the military "to execute the laws" except where the Constitution or Congress expressly allows it (18 U.S.C. 1385).
items.would: An officer removed or disciplined for refusing an election-related order, or a written order placing troops at or near polling places.

items.claim: Musk will help rig the voting machines.
items.record: The fear draws on a real remark. The day before his 2025 inauguration, Trump said Musk "knows those computers better than anybody, all those computers, those vote counting computers, and we ended up winning Pennsylvania, like, in a landslide." Snopes confirmed the quote and found no evidence he meant the win was due to Musk. Claims that Musk's Starlink network was used to steal the 2024 election were checked by AP, which called them "unfounded": election officials said their voting equipment does not use Starlink and is not connected to the internet. Musk's documented role in the midterms is money. His super PAC, which spent more than $260 million to help elect Trump in 2024, is back with a door-knocking and advertising push for Republicans. We have found no reporting or official finding that Musk, his companies, DOGE or America PAC had access to the equipment that counts or reports votes.
items.stands: Most votes cast in November will leave a paper record. In Verified Voting's 2026 survey, 69.5 percent of registered voters live where most voters mark paper ballots by hand, which the group calls "a tangible, tamper-evident and auditable record," and 1.3 percent live where every voter uses a machine with no paper record.
items.would: Documented access by Musk, his companies or DOGE to equipment or systems that count or report votes.

items.claim: They'll stage an attack to justify a crackdown.
items.record: We know of no evidence for this, and we will not speculate about it. What is documented is the use of real conditions, stretched: the "crime emergency" that put the National Guard on Washington's streets was declared while violent crime in the city was at a 30-year low, and it is now scheduled to run through January 2029.
items.stands: The limits in the two items above apply however an emergency begins: no law authorizes martial law, and troops at a polling place are a crime except to repel armed enemies of the United States.
items.would: We would report any emergency declaration and the basis it gives, and say plainly when the basis is exaggerated, as we have with the D.C. deployment.

items.claim: ICE will arrest people waiting in line to vote.
items.record: Officials will not rule out agents at polling places (see the table above), and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has said agents could be there if they are "serving a warrant on someone that we have been actively tracking down." A lawsuit by Denver and voting groups cites reports of agents at or near polling places in San Antonio, Ventura County and Syracuse this year. Border czar Tom Homan says "there is no plan for enforcement action at polling places." We have found no documented arrest of a voter at a polling place.
items.stands: Bringing "any troops or armed men" to a polling place is a federal felony unless needed "to repel armed enemies of the United States" (18 U.S.C. 592), and intimidating anyone "for the purpose of interfering with the right of such other person to vote" is a federal crime (18 U.S.C. 594). Three federal lawsuits ask the courts to keep armed federal agents away from polling places.
items.would: Armed federal agents posted at polling places on Election Day, or an arrest of a voter at one.

heard.take: Most of these fears come from people alarmed by the record above, and some of them may yet come true. We hold them to the same standard as a fraud claim anyway, because a prediction that fails costs the same credibility as a claim that falls apart. There is a second reason. Telling people the outcome is already fixed does the work of the effort this page documents: it keeps them home.

after.title: After the vote
after.sub: Election night does not decide who serves. Counties certify their counts, then states certify theirs, and the new House is seated on January 3. These are the steps, what to watch at each one, and the legal deadlines in ten states.

rows.what: Each county or local board reviews its count, a step called the canvass, and certifies the result by a deadline set in state law.
rows.watch: A board that refuses or delays. Courts have treated the duty as mandatory: an Arizona judge ruled in 2022 that the Cochise County board "exceeded its lawful authority in delaying the canvass," and a Georgia judge ruled in 2024 that the county role in certifying is "ministerial and mandatory." Michigan's law calls it "the ministerial, clerical, and nondiscretionary duty" of county canvassers. Voting groups counted "at least 17 attempts to interfere with certification during the 2024 election cycle alone," and every one of those elections was ultimately certified.

rows.what: A state board or official certifies the statewide result. Most of the ten states below set a fixed date. Texas lets its secretary of state pick a day within a window, and Pennsylvania's law sets no statewide deadline.
rows.watch: A state official who delays past the state's own deadline.

rows.what: A losing House candidate who wants to challenge the result must file notice with the House Clerk "within thirty days after the result of such election shall have been declared" (2 U.S.C. 382).

The 20th Amendment ends House terms at noon on January 3, and Congress meets that day "unless they shall by law appoint a different day." The House Clerk lists as members-elect only those "whose credentials show that they were regularly elected in accordance with the laws of their States respectively, or the laws of the United States" (2 U.S.C. 26).
rows.watch: Any attempt to keep a certified winner off the roll. Each House is "the Judge of the Elections, Returns and Qualifications of its own Members" (Art. I, Sec. 5), so the House itself rules on contested seats.
